summary: Lays out a framework of building blocks for standardizing reliable multicast transport, meaning bulk data sent from one sender to many receivers with repairs for lost packets. It is informational and sets the stage for later specifications.

eli5.summary: Reading one story aloud to a whole class is faster than telling each child separately, but you must make sure everyone heard every page. This describes the parts needed to do that online.

questions: building blocks for one to many bulk transfer
what are reliable multicast building blocks
what is a protocol core in reliable multicast
subtitle: A plan for building reliable one-to-many data transfer from reusable parts instead of one-off protocols.

tldr.problem: Reliable multicast protocols that send bulk data from one sender to many receivers each reinvent similar pieces, and the IETF expects to standardize several protocols for different needs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC splits such protocols into reusable building blocks (such as NACK-based reliability, FEC coding and congestion control) and protocol-specific cores, and lists the functional components each must cover.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational framework and a best current guess, not a standard. The building blocks in sections 4.1 to 4.3 are presented for example and design purposes.

today: RFC 3048 is an Informational RFC. It does not specify an Internet standard, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Requirements and Protocol Families
sections.content:
The document starts from RFC 2357, which sets the requirements for reliable multicast protocols the IETF will consider: congestion control, scalability and security. Congestion control means a protocol must get good throughput and good link utilization and must not starve competing flows.

Secondary requirements come from RFC 2887. They include ordering guarantees, receiver scalability (a typical group could have at least 1,000 to 10,000 receivers, possibly millions), real-time feedback, delivery guarantees, network topologies and group membership.

Following RFC 2887, the RFC sorts existing protocols into four families: NACK only, tree based ACK, Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC) and router assist. It notes that the split is not exact, and real protocols may mix mechanisms.
sections.eli5: Before building a school bus system, you write down what it must do: be safe, carry lots of kids and not block other traffic. Then you look at the different kinds of buses people already use.

sections.title: Why Building Blocks
sections.content:
The RFC defines its terms. A building block is a constituent of a protocol that implements one component, more than one, or a part of one. A protocol core is the functionality needed for a complete protocol that no building block specifies.

The advantages listed are specification reuse, reduced complexity, less verification and debugging time, easier future upgrades, common diagnostics, less effort for new protocols and parallel development.

The risks are just as plain: defining the APIs between modules delays development, too many modules increase total complexity, each extra API adds processing overhead, and re-engineering components risks abandoning prior work on protocols such as RMTP-II, SRM and PGM.

To balance this, a building block must have wide applicability, simplicity (no new fundamental research to define its APIs) and good performance (avoid breaking up the common-case packet path).
sections.eli5: Building with Lego bricks lets you reuse pieces and fix one brick at a time. But if you use too many tiny bricks, the model gets harder to put together.

sections.title: Protocol Components
sections.content:
Section 3 decomposes bulk-data reliable multicast into functional components: data reliability (loss detection and notification, loss recovery, loss protection), congestion control (congestion feedback, rate regulation, receiver controls), security, group membership, session management and tree configuration.

Loss detection can use TRACKs (tree-based positive acknowledgements), NACKs (negative acknowledgements) or both. Loss recovery sends copies of lost packets or FEC packets. Loss protection sends FEC packets in advance so some losses never become loss events at all.

The security discussion starts from the IP multicast model, where any host may join a group and receive its traffic. A protocol must therefore consider sender authentication, data encryption, transport protection and group key management. The text also notes that Source Specific Multicast gives more protection, but additional protections are still recommended.
sections.eli5: Sending a message to a whole class involves noticing who missed a word, repeating it, not talking so fast that the room gets overwhelmed, and keeping strangers out of the room. Each job is a separate component.

sections.title: The Recommended Building Blocks
sections.content:
A building block is defined as a logical protocol component that results in explicit APIs for use by other building blocks or by the protocol client. The list is the authors' "best current guess" and not meant to be exhaustive.

  • NACK-based reliability: loss detection and recovery, with suppression (multicast NACKs, or unicast NACKs with multicast confirmation) to prevent feedback implosion.
  • FEC coding: FEC codec selection and FEC packet naming for both proactive and reactive repair.
  • Congestion control: probably several versions, either source-based single-rate or receiver-driven multiple-rate.
  • Generic router support: a signaling protocol plus router algorithms, such as feedback aggregation and constrained retransmission.
  • Tree configuration: building a logical tree of aggregation agents that matches the routing topology.
  • Data security: left to IRTF research for now.
  • Common headers: recommendations on header fields protocols should share.

Everything not covered by a building block belongs in a protocol core specific to each protocol.
sections.eli5: The authors list the standard Lego sets they think will be most useful, such as one for asking for repeats and one for slowing down when the room is crowded. Anything unusual is built into each protocol by itself.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The security section points back to RFC 2357, which requires reliable multicast Internet-Drafts to explicitly explore the security aspects of the design. Building block work must examine denial-of-service attacks on and by building blocks, in addition to data security.

For IANA, the RFC proposes a building block registry using the "Specification Required" policy from RFC 2434. A registration would carry a building block name, a version number, a brief text description, a specification RFC number and a responsible person. The registry starts empty, because the blocks in sections 4.1 to 4.3 are for example and design purposes.
sections.eli5: Anyone making a new building block must think about bad guys, and an official list at IANA will keep track of every block that gets approved.

cells: NACKs request retransmission; no network infrastructure needed
Positive ACKs, with servers in the network to avoid ACK implosion
Sender-based FEC with no feedback from receivers
NACKs plus new router software for constrained NACKs and retransmissions
